description: We're Jan Burda, Lucie Vávrová and Ladislav Vávra, three students at Charles University in Prague. We love a good challenge and are curious about space, remote sensing and Earth observation. We're fascinated by what satellite data can tell us about our planet and the impact it can have. We created POLAR CHANGE to make these data easier to explore. We'd love to meet people interested in coding, geography, climate science or bringing fresh ideas.
summary:
POLAR CHANGE is an interactive web application that makes the changing sea ice conditions of our planet’s polar regions easier to explore and understand. Using historical sea-ice concentration data from NOAA/NSIDC, the project visualizes weekly changes across the Arctic and Antarctic from 1978 to 2026.

The application allows users to explore both polar regions side by side, choose independent time periods, and animate changes over time. Interactive maps and time-series charts reveal how sea ice concentration evolves across different seasons and years. Users can also export map snapshots and animations to share their findings.

By transforming complex satellite derived datasets into an accessible visual experience, POLAR CHANGE helps make decades of polar change tangible. Our goal is to encourage curiosity, support climate awareness, and make Earth observation data easier to explore for everyone.
details:
A major part of developing POLAR CHANGE was finding a way to work efficiently with decades of large scientific datasets while preserving the original spatial information.

Our data pipeline starts with daily NetCDF files from the NOAA/NSIDC Sea Ice Concentration Climate Data Record (G02202, Version 6). We process the daily measurements into weekly averages, using Monday-to-Sunday periods to provide a consistent time series. To reduce storage requirements and improve loading performance, we extract a 304 × 304 pixel region from each polar grid and encode the data using 4-bit packing, allowing two pixel values to be stored in a single byte. The processed datasets are then organized in Zarr v2 format for efficient access by the application.

One of our key technical decisions was to preserve the native polar grid without regridding or spatial interpolation. This avoids introducing additional transformations into the source data. We also had to consider missing values, consistent time periods, data compression, and responsive playback when working with a large historical dataset.

The application was built in Python, using Streamlit for the web interface and Plotly for interactive charts and visualizations. We also implemented animation controls and optimized playback so that map updates do not require the entire application to reload.

What makes our approach creative is the combination of scientific data processing and an accessible, exploratory interface. Rather than simplifying the underlying data into a few predefined conclusions, we give users the freedom to investigate spatial and temporal patterns themselves.

We hope this approach can support climate education, inspire further exploration of Earth observation data, and demonstrate how open scientific datasets can be transformed into useful and engaging tools.
